optionAnalysis.reason: Starting with $T_1$ (`bba`, length 3) ignores the longer $T_3$ match `bbaac` (length 5).
`bba`·`aca`·`bc` is a valid split into $T_1T_1T_3$, but it is not longest-match: $T_3$ matches the longer prefix `bbaac` first.
$T_2$ matches only `bb` (length 2), shorter than $T_3$'s 5.
Maximal munch gives `bbaac` ($T_3$) then `abc` ($T_3$).

cse-2018-cs-38.approach: In a parse tree the operator deeper in the tree binds tighter (higher precedence); a chain of the same operator growing on the left side means left associativity, growing on the right side means right associativity.

steps.title: Precedence
steps.body: The \$ nodes sit below the # nodes: the tree groups $b\,\$\,c\,\$\,d$ into one subtree before any # is applied. So \$ has **higher precedence** than #.

steps.title: Associativity of \$
steps.body: `b$c$d` is parsed as $(b\,\$\,c)\,\$\,d$ — the inner \$ is the **left** child. So \$ is **left associative**.

steps.title: Associativity of #
steps.body: The # chain is $a\,\#\,\big((b\$c\$d)\,\#\,(e\,\#\,f)\big)$ — each # has the next # as its **right** child. So # is **right associative**.

answer.value: \$ has higher precedence and is left associative; # is right associative

optionAnalysis.reason: Matches all three observations: \$ deeper, \$ nests left, # nests right.
The # operator is near the root, so it has lower precedence; \$ nests to the left, not right.
The # operator nests to the right (e#f is the right child), so it is right associative.
The # operator does not have higher precedence — the \$ subtrees are below it.

pitfalls: Confusing 'closer to root' with 'higher precedence' — it is the opposite.
cse-2018-cs-38.verification: Fully parenthesised: $a\#(((b\$c)\$d)\#(e\#f))$, consistent with option A's grammar.

cse-2018-cs-39.approach: Apply the Banker's safety algorithm: compute Need = Max − Allocation, then repeatedly pick any process whose Need fits in Work, let it finish and release its allocation.

steps.title: Run P1 then P3
steps.body:
P1 needs $(1,0,2)\le(5,3,4)$ ✓, releases $(1,1,2)$: Work $=(6,4,6)$.

P3 needs $(3,4,1)\le(6,4,6)$ ✓, releases $(2,0,0)$: Work $=(8,4,6)$.

Safe sequence $\langle P0, P2, P1, P3\rangle$ exists ⇒ **safe state**.

answer.value: The system is in safe state

optionAnalysis.reason: The safe sequence P0, P2, P1, P3 exists with the current Available (3,3,0).
The premise 'not in safe state' is false; no extra E is needed.
The state is already safe; no extra F is needed.
Although Available G is 0, P0 needs no G and frees one, so the state is safe without extra G.

pitfalls: Stopping early because Available G is 0 — P0 needs zero G and releases one.
cse-2018-cs-39.verification: Final Work $(8,4,6)$ equals Available plus all allocations: $(3+5,\,3+1,\,0+6)$.

cse-2018-cs-40.approach: Note the swapped names: here `full` counts free slots (initially N) and `empty` counts filled slots (initially 0). The producer must wait for a free slot and announce a filled one; the consumer does the reverse.

steps.title: Producer
steps.body: Before adding it needs a free slot ⇒ `wait(full)` (P = full). After adding, one more item is readable ⇒ `signal(empty)` (Q = empty).

steps.title: Consumer
steps.body: Before consuming it needs an item ⇒ `wait(empty)` (R = empty; initially 0, so the consumer blocks on an empty buffer). After consuming, one slot is free ⇒ `signal(full)` (S = full).

steps.title: Result
steps.body: P: full, Q: empty, R: empty, S: full.

answer.value: P: full, Q: empty, R: empty, S: full

optionAnalysis.reason: Producer signals `full` (free slots) after filling one, so free slots never decrease and overflow is possible; consumer never frees slots.
Producer waits on `empty` (initially 0) and consumer on `full`; consumer can read from an empty buffer.
Producer waits for a free slot and signals an item; consumer waits for an item and signals a free slot.
Producer waits on `empty` (0) and blocks forever at start; roles are reversed.

pitfalls: Using the textbook meaning of `empty`/`full`; the question deliberately swaps them.
cse-2018-cs-40.verification: Initial values check: producer can proceed N times before blocking (full = N); consumer blocks at start (empty = 0).

cse-2018-cs-41.approach: Because r.B is a foreign key into s, every r tuple has a matching s tuple, so r LOJ s equals r ⋈ s. The only query that differs is the one that left-joins r with a *filtered* s, keeping unmatched r tuples padded with nulls.

steps.title: Q keeps only B < 5
steps.body: $Q = r\bowtie\sigma_{B<5}(s)$ contains exactly the r tuples with $B<5$, each joined with its s tuple.

steps.title: Check A, B, D
steps.body:
- **A:** $\sigma_{B<5}(r\bowtie s)$ — selection pushes through the join ⇒ same as Q.
- **B:** with the foreign key, $r\ \text{LOJ}\ s = r\bowtie s$ (no dangling r tuples), then the same selection ⇒ same as Q.
- **D:** $\sigma_{B<5}(r)\ \text{LOJ}\ s$ — every selected r tuple matches s, so this is $\sigma_{B<5}(r)\bowtie s$ ⇒ same as Q.

steps.title: C differs
steps.body: $r\ \text{LOJ}\ \sigma_{B<5}(s)$: an r tuple with $B\ge5$ finds no partner in the filtered s but is still kept, with $C=$ NULL. Q drops it, so **C is not equivalent**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Selection on the join attribute commutes with the join; equivalent to Q.
Foreign key makes LOJ identical to the inner join; equivalent after the selection.
Keeps r tuples with $B\ge5$ padded with NULL; Q excludes them.
Filtered r tuples all have matches in s, so the LOJ adds no NULL rows; equivalent.

pitfalls: Forgetting that filtering the right operand of a left outer join creates dangling left tuples.
cse-2018-cs-41.verification: Counter-example: r = {(1,7)}, s = {(7,x)}. Q is empty; C returns (1,7,NULL).

cse-2018-cs-42.approach: For each schema find the candidate keys, then test every FD X → A: BCNF needs X to be a superkey; 3NF also accepts A being a prime attribute.

steps.title: Schema I
steps.body: `courses` is set-valued, so the relation is not even in 1NF (hence not in 3NF). Answer cannot be I.

steps.title: Schema II
steps.body: Keys: {rollno, courseid} and, since email → rollno, also {email, courseid}. FD email → rollno: email is not a superkey ⇒ **violates BCNF**; but rollno is prime ⇒ **3NF holds**. Other FD has a key on the left. So II is in 3NF but not BCNF.

steps.title: Schemas III and IV
steps.body:
III: marks → grade, marks not a superkey, grade non-prime ⇒ transitive dependency, **not 3NF**.

IV: courseid → credit, courseid is a proper part of the key and credit is non-prime ⇒ partial dependency, **not 2NF/3NF**.

optionAnalysis.reason: A set-valued attribute breaks 1NF, so Schema I is not in 3NF.
email → rollno has a non-superkey LHS (fails BCNF) but a prime RHS (passes 3NF).
marks → grade is a transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute; not 3NF.
courseid → credit is a partial dependency; not even 2NF.

pitfalls: Missing the second candidate key {email, courseid} in Schema II, which is what makes rollno prime.
cse-2018-cs-42.verification: Closure: {email, courseid}+ = {email, rollno, courseid}, confirming it is a key and rollno is prime.

cse-2018-cs-43.approach: A permutation of 100 numbers has 99 adjacent positions to swap, giving the degree; adjacent swaps (bubble-sort moves) can turn any permutation into any other, so the graph is connected.

steps.title: Degree y
steps.body: Swapping positions $(i, i+1)$ for $i=1,\dots,99$ gives 99 distinct neighbours. So $y=99$.

steps.title: Components z
steps.body: Bubble sort reaches the identity from any permutation using only adjacent swaps, so every vertex is connected to the identity ⇒ $z=1$.

pitfalls: Counting $\binom{100}{2}$ swaps — only *adjacent* swaps are edges.
Thinking parity splits the graph into 2 components; each adjacent swap changes parity, so it links both classes.
cse-2018-cs-43.verification: Small case n = 3: 6 vertices, each of degree 2, forming one 6-cycle — $y=n-1$, $z=1$.

cse-2018-cs-44.approach: Bayes' theorem: find P(H_D) by total probability over Guwahati's three states, then divide the H_G term by it.

steps.title: Bayes
steps.body: $P(H_G\mid H_D) = \dfrac{P(H_D\mid H_G)P(H_G)}{P(H_D)} = \dfrac{0.080}{0.133} = 0.6015\ldots \approx 0.60$

pitfalls: Answering $P(H_D\mid H_G)=0.40$ directly instead of reversing the condition.
cse-2018-cs-44.verification: $P(M_G\mid H_D)=0.05/0.133\approx0.376$, $P(L_G\mid H_D)=0.003/0.133\approx0.023$; the three posteriors sum to 1.

cse-2018-cs-45.approach: For a fixed y ≠ 1, the inner recursion halves x from 1024 to 1, printing once per halving; then y drops by 1 and x resets to 1024. Multiply prints per y-value by the number of y-values.

steps.title: Prints per value of y
steps.body: With $y\ne1$, $x$ goes $1024\to512\to\dots\to2\to1$: one `*` per halving, i.e. $\log_2 1024 = 10$ prints. At $x=1$ the else branch sets $y=y-1$ and calls `Count(1024, y)`.

steps.title: Number of y values
steps.body: The prints happen for $y = 1024, 1023, \dots, 2$ — that is $1023$ values. When $y=1$ the function stops.

pitfalls: Counting 1024 y-values; the call with $y=1$ prints nothing.
Counting 11 prints per round (x = 1 does not print).
cse-2018-cs-45.verification: Check with Count(4,3): y=3 prints 2, y=2 prints 2 ⇒ 4 = (3−1)·log₂4.

cse-2018-cs-46.approach: A 7-node heap is a complete tree with two 3-node subtrees. The root must be 1; choose which 3 of the remaining 6 values go left, and each 3-node subtree has 2 valid heap shapes.

steps.title: Root and split
steps.body: Root = 1. The other 6 values split into left and right subtrees of 3 each: $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ ways.

steps.title: Each 3-node subtree
steps.body: Its smallest value must be the subtree root; the other two can be placed as left/right children in $2! = 2$ ways.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $20 \times 2 \times 2 = 80$.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the 7-node heap shape is fixed (perfect tree), so only value placement varies.

cse-2018-cs-47.approach: Build the MST with Kruskal and look for ties: the cheap edges 1 and 3 are forced, the left vertex has two weight-4 options, and the right vertex gets two options exactly when x equals 5.
cse-2018-cs-47.given: Label the vertices T (top), L (left), R (right), BL (bottom-left), BR (bottom-right). Edges: T–BL 1, T–BR 3, T–L 4, L–BL 4, BL–BR 4, R–BR 5, T–R x.

steps.title: Forced cheap edges
steps.body: Kruskal takes T–BL (1) and T–BR (3) — every MST contains them (each is the unique lightest edge of a cut).

scene.caption: T–BL (1) and T–BR (3) are in every MST

steps.title: Weight-4 edges
steps.body: BL–BR (4) would close the cycle T–BL–BR, so it is never used. L can be attached by T–L (4) **or** L–BL (4): **2 choices**, each giving the same weight.

scene.caption: L joins via either weight-4 edge: 2 ways

steps.title: Choose x
steps.body:
R is joined by T–R ($x$) or R–BR (5).
- $x<5$ or $x>5$: one choice (the cheaper edge).
- $x=5$: both are minimum ⇒ **2 choices**.

So $x=5$ maximizes the count.

scene.caption: With x = 5, R joins via either weight-5 edge: 2 ways

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Choices for L and R are independent: $2 \times 2 = 4$ MWSTs (each of weight $1+3+4+5=13$).

pitfalls: Including BL–BR (4) as a third option for L — it does not touch L and forms a cycle with T–BL and T–BR.
cse-2018-cs-47.verification: Enumerated: {T-BL, T-BR} + {T-L or L-BL} + {T-R or R-BR} — exactly 4 trees, all of weight 13.

cse-2018-cs-48.approach: Compute value/weight ratios, run the greedy fill, and find the true optimum by checking the few feasible subsets under 11 kg.

steps.title: Greedy
steps.body: Take item 4 (2 kg, ₹24). Item 1 needs 10 kg, $2+10=12>11$ ⇒ skip. Item 3: $2+4=6$ kg ⇒ take (₹20). Item 2: $6+7=13>11$ ⇒ skip. $V_{greedy}=24+20=44$.

pitfalls: Using fractional greedy (splitting item 1) — items cannot be split here.
cse-2018-cs-48.verification: DP over capacity 11 also gives 60 (item 1 alone).

cse-2018-cs-49.approach: Concept tested: **essential prime implicants with don't-cares**. Use the Xs to form the largest PIs, then count the PIs that are the only cover of some **1**-cell (a don't-care never makes a PI essential).

steps.title: Prime implicants
steps.body: Using the Xs: $\overline{Q}\,\overline{S}$ (0, 2, 8, 10), $P\overline{Q}$ (8, 9, 10, 11), $\overline{Q}R$ (2, 3, 10, 11), $\overline{P}QS$ (5, 7), $\overline{P}RS$ (3, 7). ($P\overline{S}$ = 8, 10, 12, 14 is made of Xs only, so it covers no 1 and is never used.)

steps.title: Distinguished 1-cells
steps.body: $m_0$: only $\overline{Q}\,\overline{S}$. $m_5$: only $\overline{P}QS$. $m_9$: only $P\overline{Q}$. ($m_2$, $m_7$, $m_{11}$ each lie in two PIs.)

steps.title: Count
steps.body: 3 essential PIs. They already cover every 1, so $F = \overline{Q}\,\overline{S} + \overline{P}QS + P\overline{Q}$.

cse-2018-cs-49.shortcut: Look at the 1s with the fewest 1/X neighbours: $m_0$, $m_5$, $m_9$ each have one maximal loop.
pitfalls: Counting a PI as essential because it is the only one through some don't-care cell: essential is decided by 1-cells only.
Forgetting that the Xs can make the corner quad.
cse-2018-cs-49.verification: Quine–McCluskey with the don't-cares, then a chart over the six 1-cells only: single-mark columns 0, 5, 9.

cse-2018-cs-50.approach: With no hazards, the PO stage is the bottleneck: it is busy continuously once the first instruction arrives. Total time = cycles before the first PO + total PO cycles + the final WB.

steps.title: Before PO
steps.body: Instruction 1 does IF, ID, OF in cycles 1–3 and enters PO in cycle 4. The front stages (1 cycle each) always have the next instruction ready, so PO never idles.

steps.title: PO busy time
steps.body: $40\times3 + 35\times2 + 25\times1 = 120 + 70 + 25 = 215$ cycles, occupying cycles $4$ to $3+215=218$.

steps.title: Last WB
steps.body: The last instruction writes back in cycle $219$. Total $= 3 + 215 + 1 = 219$.

pitfalls: Using $k + n - 1$ with the maximum stage time (that assumes every instruction takes 3 cycles in PO).
cse-2018-cs-50.verification: Equivalently: sum of PO times + (number of other stages) $= 215 + 4 = 219$.

cse-2018-cs-51.approach: Expanding opcode: measure the 16-bit encoding space in units of 2^10, subtract what Types 1–3 use, and divide the remainder by the 2^6 encodings each 1F instruction consumes.

steps.title: Operand widths
steps.body: Integer register: $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits; FP register: $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits. Instruction: 16 bits ⇒ $2^{16}$ encodings.

steps.title: Type-4
steps.body: Left: $2^{16} - 62\times2^{10} = (64-62)\times2^{10} = 2048$ encodings. Each 1F instruction uses $2^6 = 64$ of them: $N = 2048/64 = 32$.

pitfalls: Giving each type a fixed-width opcode field instead of sharing the encoding space.
cse-2018-cs-51.verification: In opcode-bit terms: 4 bits for Type-1 leave 12 patterns; Type-2 uses 8 ⇒ 4 left; extending by 2 bits gives 16, Type-3 uses 14 ⇒ 2 left; extending by 4 bits gives $2\times16=32$.

cse-2018-cs-52.approach: Read L1 off the automaton (ε plus odd-length strings of 0), then compute successive powers until they stop changing.

steps.title: L1 from the automaton
steps.body: Start state is accepting ⇒ $\varepsilon\in L_1$. The second state is reached after 1, 3, 5, … zeros and is accepting; the third (after 2, 4, … zeros, except 0) is not. So $L_1 = \{\varepsilon\}\cup\{0^{2k+1} \mid k\ge0\}$.

steps.title: Powers
steps.body:
- $L^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$
- $L^1 = L_1 = \{\varepsilon, 0, 000, \dots\}$ — no $00$, so $L^1\ne L^0$.
- $L^2 = L_1L_1$: contains $L_1$ (since $\varepsilon\in L_1$) and odd+odd = all even lengths $\ge2$, so $L^2 = 0^*$; $L^2\ne L^1$.
- $L^3 = L^2L_1 = 0^*$ since $0^*\cdot L_1 = 0^*$.

steps.title: Order
steps.body: Smallest $k$ with $L^k=L^{k+1}$ is $k=2$.

pitfalls: Reading the automaton as accepting even lengths; the second (accepting) state is reached after an odd number of zeros.
cse-2018-cs-52.verification: $00\notin L^1$ but $00 = 0\cdot0\in L^2$, and $L^2=0^*$ is closed under further concatenation.

cse-2018-cs-53.approach: Only cylinder numbers matter. Run SSTF from cylinder 80, add up the cylinders travelled and count direction reversals, then convert: 20 mW per 100 cylinders and 15 mW per reversal.
cse-2018-cs-53.given: Requested cylinders: 72, 134, 20, 86, 116, 16. Head at 80, moving up.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: Movement: $\frac{200}{100}\times20 = 40$ mW. Reversals: $3\times15 = 45$ mW. Total $= 40+45 = 85$ mW.

pitfalls: Counting the first move 80 → 86 as a reversal — the head was already moving up.
Including sector/platter switching, which the question says is negligible.

cse-2018-cs-54.approach: The TCP header is just data to IP. Each fragment can carry at most MTU − 20 bytes of data, rounded down to a multiple of 8; the offset field counts 8-byte units.

steps.title: Data per fragment
steps.body: IP payload $= 4500 - 20 = 4480$ bytes. Max data per fragment $= 600 - 20 = 580$, rounded down to a multiple of 8 ⇒ $576$ bytes.

steps.title: Offsets
steps.body: Fragment 1: offset $0$. Fragment 2: $576/8 = 72$. Fragment 3: $2\times576/8 = 1152/8 = 144$.

pitfalls: Subtracting the 40-byte TCP header from each fragment — only the first fragment contains it, as ordinary data.
Using 580 (not a multiple of 8).

cse-2018-cs-55.approach: Q avoids a collision only if it hears P's signal while still carrier-sensing. Q senses during t = 0 to 5, so P's signal must reach Q within 5 time units: d/10 ≤ 5.

steps.title: Timeline
steps.body: P starts sending at $t=0$. Q senses from $t=0$ to $t=5$ and, if it hears nothing, transmits right after. P's signal reaches Q at $t = d/10$.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: Q defers (and so avoids a collision) iff the signal arrives inside the sensing window: $\dfrac{d}{10} \le 5 \Rightarrow d \le 50$ m.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Maximum $d = 50$ m. For larger $d$, Q finishes sensing before P's signal arrives, starts sending, and the two transmissions overlap.

pitfalls: Using the 20-unit transmission time — it does not matter for whether Q hears P in time.
cse-2018-cs-55.verification: At $d=50$ the signal arrives at $t=5$, the last sensing instant; at $d=60$ it arrives at $t=6$, after Q has already started.
